title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip in System Design Interviews
summary: Ten database concepts for system design interviews, ordered from foundational to advanced: indexing, transactions, ACID, locking, isolation levels, MVCC, connection pooling, partitioning, replication and sharding. Each one gets a worked example, trade-offs and an interview takeaway.

chapters.title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip
points: Cover promise: 10 database concepts that come up in almost every system design interview
1. Indexing: find rows without scanning the whole table
2. Transactions: group statements into one all-or-nothing unit
3. ACID: the four guarantees a transaction gives you
4. Locking: how concurrent writers avoid clobbering each other
5. Isolation Levels: how much concurrent work a transaction can see
6. MVCC: readers and writers coexist using row versions
7. Connection Pooling: reuse a few expensive connections for many requests
8. Partitioning: split one big table into smaller pieces on one server
9. Replication: copy data to other nodes for availability and read scale
10. Sharding: spread data across servers to scale writes and storage
Order of the series: single-node basics first, then concurrency, then scaling out across machines
Each chapter follows one pattern: what it is, why it exists, used for, how it works, benefits, things to consider, interview takeaway

chapters.title: Indexing
points: What it is: a separate sorted structure, usually a B-tree, that maps column values to row locations so lookups skip the full table scan
Why it exists: scanning 10M rows is O(n), while a B-tree lookup is O(log n) and takes about 3-4 page reads
Used for: WHERE filters, JOIN keys, ORDER BY, and enforcing UNIQUE on columns like email or user_id
How it works: table users(id, email, created_at) with 10M rows; SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@x.com' runs a Seq Scan in about 800 ms
How it works: CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email); the plan becomes an Index Scan in about 0.1 ms (root, internal page, leaf, then the heap row)
How it works: a composite index (user_id, created_at) serves WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at, by the leftmost-prefix rule
Benefit: reads drop from O(n) to O(log n), and the same index makes sorts and range scans cheap
Benefit: a covering index (CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (name)) answers a query from the index alone, with no table lookup
Consider: every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also update every index, so write cost and storage grow with each one
Consider: low-cardinality columns (a boolean) and expressions like WHERE lower(email) = ... skip the index unless it is built on that expression
Interview takeaway: index the columns in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY, confirm with EXPLAIN, and avoid over-indexing write-heavy tables

chapters.title: Transactions
points: What it is: a group of statements the database treats as one logical unit that fully succeeds (COMMIT) or fully undoes (ROLLBACK)
Why it exists: a crash or error halfway through a multi-step change would otherwise leave data half-updated
Used for: money transfers, order placement plus stock decrement, and any change that touches more than one row or table
How it works: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT;
How it works: if the second UPDATE fails, ROLLBACK restores account 1 to its original balance, so no money vanishes
How it works: savepoints (SAVEPOINT s1; ROLLBACK TO s1) undo only part of a transaction
Benefit: the application never sees a half-finished state
Benefit: error handling gets simpler, because one ROLLBACK undoes everything
Consider: long transactions hold locks and bloat logs, so keep them short and never wait on user input inside one
Consider: a transaction spans one database; across services you need sagas or two-phase commit
Interview takeaway: explain the transfer example, say 'all or nothing', and mention keeping transactions short

chapters.title: ACID
points: What it is: four guarantees of a reliable transaction: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Why it exists: to give applications predictable behavior despite crashes, power loss and concurrent users
Used for: banking, payments, inventory and bookings, where wrong data costs real money
How it works: Atomicity is all or nothing, implemented with an undo log
How it works: Consistency means a commit moves the database from one valid state to another, enforced by constraints (CHECK bal >= 0, foreign keys)
How it works: Isolation hides partial work from concurrent transactions, and its strength is tunable
How it works: Durability means that once COMMIT returns, the data survives a crash, because the write-ahead log (WAL) is fsynced first
Worked example: INSERT of a 100 USD order returns OK, the server loses power, and after restart WAL replay brings the order back
Benefit: predictable, correct data under failure and concurrency
Consider: ACID costs throughput; many NoSQL stores relax it for speed and scale, as in BASE
Interview takeaway: give one sentence and one failure scenario for each letter, and note that 'C' in ACID differs from 'C' in CAP

chapters.title: Locking
points: What it is: a mechanism that makes a transaction hold a claim on a row or table so others must wait or fail
Why it exists: two transactions updating the same row at once would produce lost updates
Used for: protecting counters, balances and inventory under concurrent writes
How it works: shared (read) locks allow many readers; exclusive (write) locks allow one writer and block the others
How it works: two users buy the last ticket; SELECT stock FROM tickets WHERE id = 5 FOR UPDATE; takes a row lock
How it works: the second transaction waits at its own FOR UPDATE until the first commits, then sees stock = 0 and refuses the sale
How it works: optimistic locking adds a version column: UPDATE ... SET qty = 4, ver = 8 WHERE id = 5 AND ver = 7, and retries if 0 rows changed
Benefit: guarantees correctness for hot rows without extra infrastructure
Benefit: optimistic locking gives high throughput when conflicts are rare
Consider: deadlocks, where T1 waits on T2 and T2 on T1; the database aborts one victim, so take locks in a consistent order and retry
Consider: long-held locks serialize traffic, and table-level locks block all writers
Interview takeaway: choose pessimistic for high contention and optimistic for low contention, and name deadlock as the risk

chapters.title: Isolation Levels
points: What it is: a setting that decides how much of other transactions' concurrent work a transaction can see
Why it exists: full isolation is slow, so databases let you trade correctness for concurrency
Used for: tuning each workload, such as a reporting query versus a payment write
How it works: anomalies are dirty read (uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (a row changes between two reads), phantom read (new rows appear in a repeated range query)
How it works: Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads; Read Committed blocks them and is the default in PostgreSQL and Oracle
How it works: Repeatable Read blocks non-repeatable reads and is MySQL InnoDB's default; Serializable blocks all anomalies, as if transactions ran one by one
How it works: T1 reads balance 500; T2 sets it to 400 and commits; T1 rereads 400 under Read Committed but 500 under Repeatable Read
How it works: set per transaction with SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
Benefit: you pick the cheapest level that is still correct for each workload
Consider: Serializable can abort transactions with serialization failures, so the app must retry
Consider: Repeatable Read can still permit write skew, such as two doctors both going off-call
Interview takeaway: recite the four levels with the anomaly each one blocks, and state the default of the database in question

chapters.title: MVCC
points: What it is: Multi-Version Concurrency Control, where the database keeps several versions of a row and each transaction reads a consistent snapshot
Why it exists: with plain locks, readers block writers and writers block readers
Used for: PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB and Oracle, to implement Read Committed and Repeatable Read without read locks
How it works: each row version carries a creator transaction ID (xmin) and a deleter ID (xmax); a snapshot sees only versions committed before it began
How it works: row price = 10 (xmin=100); at txn 120 an UPDATE to 12 writes a new version (xmin=120) and marks the old one xmax=120
How it works: a reader whose snapshot started at txn 110 still reads 10; a reader starting after 120 commits reads 12
Benefit: readers never block writers and writers never block readers, so throughput is high
Benefit: snapshot reads give a stable, consistent view for long reports
Consider: old versions pile up (bloat), so PostgreSQL needs VACUUM and InnoDB needs undo purge
Consider: writers touching the same row still conflict, and long-running transactions stop old-version cleanup
Interview takeaway: 'readers don't block writers because each reads its own snapshot'; the cost is vacuum and storage

chapters.title: Connection Pooling
points: What it is: a cache of open database connections that requests borrow and return instead of opening a new one each time
Why it exists: opening a connection costs a TCP and TLS handshake plus auth, about 20-50 ms, and PostgreSQL spends roughly 10 MB of RAM per connection
Used for: web servers and serverless functions making many short queries
How it works: 500 app requests per second against PostgreSQL with max_connections = 100
How it works: without a pool, connections are exhausted and errors appear; with a pool of size 20, requests borrow a connection, run about 5 ms, and return it
How it works: settings are max size, min idle, acquire timeout (such as 3 s) and idle timeout; tools include HikariCP, PgBouncer and RDS Proxy
How it works: sizing rule of thumb is (CPU cores x 2) + effective disk spindles, and bigger is not faster
Benefit: removes handshake latency from every request
Benefit: caps database load, which protects it from connection storms
Consider: pool exhaustion when connections leak or transactions run long, because requests queue then time out
Consider: PgBouncer transaction mode breaks session state such as prepared statements and temp tables
Interview takeaway: a small pool in front of the database beats many connections; always release connections in a finally block

chapters.title: Partitioning
points: What it is: splitting one large table into smaller partitions inside the same database server, by a partition key
Why it exists: giant tables make queries, index maintenance and deletes slow
Used for: time-series logs, orders by month, and data retention
How it works: types are range (by date), list (by region), hash (by user_id modulo N)
How it works: CREATE TABLE events (id bigint, ts date, ...) PARTITION BY RANGE (ts); partitions events_2026_09 and events_2026_10
How it works: SELECT ... WHERE ts = '2026-10-06' prunes to events_2026_10 only, so 11 of 12 monthly partitions are never read
How it works: dropping old data becomes DROP TABLE events_2025_01, which is instant, instead of a huge DELETE
Benefit: partition pruning and smaller per-partition indexes make queries faster
Benefit: cheap archival and maintenance, since each partition is vacuumed or reindexed separately
Consider: queries that omit the partition key scan every partition
Consider: a skewed key creates uneven partitions, and unique constraints must include the key
Interview takeaway: partitioning is one machine and sharding is many machines; pick a key you filter on often

chapters.title: Replication
points: What it is: continuously copying data from a primary node to one or more replicas on other servers
Why it exists: for fault tolerance, read scaling, and lower latency by placing replicas near users
Used for: failover, read-heavy apps, analytics replicas, and backups
How it works: single-leader sends writes to the primary and reads to replicas; multi-leader and leaderless (Dynamo-style) designs also exist
How it works: synchronous replication waits for the replica before ack (no data loss, higher latency); asynchronous acks immediately (fast, but replicas lag)
How it works: a primary in us-east-1 with 2 replicas; a user writes a profile and reads it from a replica 300 ms behind, so the old value shows
How it works: fix read-your-writes by routing that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after a write
Benefit: if the primary dies, a replica is promoted and the system stays up (failover)
Benefit: reads scale horizontally by adding replicas
Consider: replication lag causes stale reads, and async failover can lose recent writes
Consider: replication does not scale writes, since every write still hits the one primary, and split-brain is a risk if two nodes both lead
Interview takeaway: replication scales reads and availability, not writes; name the sync versus async trade-off and the lag problem

chapters.title: Sharding
points: What it is: horizontally splitting data across multiple independent database servers (shards), each holding a subset of rows
Why it exists: one server runs out of disk, memory or write throughput, and replication cannot fix write limits
Used for: very large systems such as social feeds, chat, and multi-tenant SaaS
How it works: strategies are range-based (user_id 1-1M on shard A), hash-based (hash(user_id) mod N), and directory/lookup-based
How it works: 4 shards, shard = user_id % 4; user 10 maps to shard 2 and user 13 to shard 1
How it works: adding a fifth shard remaps most keys with plain modulo, so consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of the keys
Benefit: write throughput and storage grow almost linearly with shard count
Benefit: failures and load stay isolated to one shard
Consider: cross-shard joins and transactions are expensive or need two-phase commit
Consider: hot shards (a celebrity user) and costly resharding, so choose a high-cardinality, evenly distributed shard key
Interview takeaway: shard only after indexing, caching, replication and partitioning are exhausted, and justify the shard key

chapters.title: Database Concepts Cheatsheet
points: Indexing: B-tree turns O(n) scans into O(log n); costs writes and storage; verify with EXPLAIN
Transactions: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK make multi-statement changes all-or-nothing
ACID: atomicity (undo log), consistency (constraints), isolation, durability (WAL fsync)
Locking: pessimistic uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE; optimistic uses a version column; beware deadlocks
Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable, blocking dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads in that order
MVCC: row versions plus snapshots; readers never block writers; VACUUM cleans up old versions
Connection pooling: a small reusable pool (about cores x 2) in front of the DB; avoid leaks
Partitioning: split a table on one server by range, list or hash; prune by key
Replication: copy to replicas for read scale and failover; watch lag and sync versus async
Sharding: split data across servers by shard key to scale writes; avoid cross-shard joins
Scaling order to say aloud: index, pool, cache, replicate, partition, then shard
